Bindings

Binding a name to a value. ← is the bind glyph: the value on the right goes into the name on the left.

Fixed or writable#

let binds a name once. mut binds a name you intend to change.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let int limit ← 10
    mut int count ← 0

    count ← count + 1
    print limit, count
}

Assigning a let name a second time is a compile error (SEM020 immutable_second_assignment), not a convention. Reach for let first and widen to mut only where the value genuinely moves. const is no longer a run-time binding: it declares a compile-time fact with =, and a run-time const int x ← 1 is PARSE010 runtime_const_retired.

Type holes#

_ is a type hole: the compiler infers one concrete type for the binding. Every binding writes its type slot, so _ is how you ask for inference; there is no short form, and let name ← "Marcus" is PARSE010 binding_type_slot_required.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let _ name ← "Marcus"
    let _ numeri ← [1, 2, 3]
    print name, numeri
}

The hole infers a type; it does not make the binding dynamic. name is string from this point on.

Union types and holes#

An inline A ∪ B in type position names its union members explicitly. A standalone ∪ is a union hole: the compiler infers a finite set of member types rather than one.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
main {
    let string ∪ int mixed ← 7
    let list<string ∪ int> both ← [1, "two", 3]
    print mixed, both
}

Read a union out with match, which forces every arm to be handled.

Optional values#

T ∪ none is the optional shape. It is an ordinary union whose other member is nothing — Faber has no separate nullable syntax.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
fn primum(list<int> res) → int ∪ none {
    if res.length() ≡ 0 then return null
    return res[0]
}

main {
    print primum([1, 2, 3])
}

Destructuring#

from pulls named fields out of a class value in one statement.

+++ toml
locale = "en"

+++ faber
class Punctum {
    let int x
    let int y
}

main {
    let _ p ← Punctum { x = 1, y = 2 }
    let int x ← p.x
    let int y ← p.y
    print x, y
}

Class values are built with named fields in braces, not positional arguments — so adding a field never silently reorders an existing call site.
